notes: Chunk C (units 30-42: topics T14 to T17). Every item is a word or algebra problem with no figure given in the book; no v3 trigger applies, so no diagram is required.
Four solutions are optional (a figure would help but the LP text is complete): C81, C89, C99, C101. They are not added to the plan.
Three figure entries: the second use of the Mukta comic strip (P10) by C78, and two decorative illustrations on pages 12 and 13 that the base inventory does not list.
See map/notes_C.md for borderline calls and LP text issues.

The base id itself belongs to the section 6.6 teaching units, not to this chunk.

items.ncert_ref: Section 6.6 - Figure it Out, book Q2 (FiOC.q2)
items.question_text: In the trick given above, instead of finding the difference of the two 2 digit numbers, find their sum. What will happen? For example: 31 + 13 = 44, 28 + 82 = 110, 12 + 21 = 33. Observe that all these numbers are divisible by 11. Is this always true? Can we justify this claim using algebra?
items.reason: The question gives everything in words and numbers: the change (sum instead of difference) and three worked numeric examples (31 + 13, 28 + 82, 12 + 21). The comic strip of Mukta's trick on page 10 is not needed to attempt it and the question gives no figure of its own.

items.ncert_ref: Section 6.6 - Figure it Out, book Q5 (FiOC.q5)
items.question_text: There are 3 shrines, each with a magical pond in the front. If anyone dips flowers into these magical ponds, the number of flowers doubles. A person has some flowers. He dips them all in the first pond and then places some flowers in shrine 1. Next, he dips the remaining flowers in the second pond and places some flowers in shrine 2. Finally, he dips the remaining flowers in the third pond and then places them all in shrine 3. If he placed an equal number of flowers in each shrine, how many flowers did he start with? How many flowers did he place in each shrine?
items.reason: The book prints no figure for the shrines and ponds; the story is complete in words, and a question with no given figure gets no question diagram.

items.ncert_ref: Section 6.6 - Figure it Out, book Q6 (FiOC.q6)
items.question_text: A farm has some horses and hens. The total number of heads of these animals is 55 and the total number of legs is 150. How many horses and how many hens are on the farm? Can you solve this without letter-numbers? (Hint: If all the 55 animals were hens, then how many legs would there be? Using the difference between this number and 150, can you find the number of horses?)
items.reason: The book prints an illustration of horses and hens behind a fence with a boy peeking in (page 12). It carries no counts or other data (a few heads are visible, not 55), and the numbers 55 and 150 are in the text.

items.ncert_ref: Section 6.6 - Figure it Out, book Q6 (FiOC.q6)
items.question_text: A farm has some horses and hens. The total number of heads of these animals is 55 and the total number of legs is 150. How many horses and how many hens are on the farm? Can you solve this without letter-numbers? (Hint: If all the 55 animals were hens, then how many legs would there be? Using the difference between this number and 150, can you find the number of horses?)
items.reason: Equation 4h + 2(55 - h) = 150 and the all-hens argument 55 x 2 = 110, 150 - 110 = 40, 40 / 2 = 20 are plain arithmetic; the answer is two numbers, not a picture.

items.ncert_ref: Section 6.6 - Figure it Out, book Q11 (FiOC.q11)
items.question_text: Karim and the Genie. Each time Karim goes around the banyan tree, the coins in his pocket double, and then he gives the genie 8 coins. After the third round the coins doubled, and he was left with only 8 coins, exactly the number he owed the genie. (i) How many coins did Karim initially have? How should the genie set the cost per round so that it gets all of Karim's coins?
items.reason: The book prints an illustration of Karim walking round the banyan tree with the genie sitting on top (page 13). It carries no numbers or data; every number is in the text.
